fetched_contents.text: Energy output modalities of shockwave lithotripsy in the treatment of urinary stones: escalating or fixed voltage? A systematic review and meta-analysis World J Urol. 2020 Oct;38(10):2443-2453. doi: 10.1007/s00345-019-03049-2. Epub 2019 Dec 7. Authors Affiliations * 1 Department of Urology, Minimally Invasive Surgery Center, The First Affiliated Hospital of Guangzhou Medical University, Kangda Road 1#, Haizhu District, Guangzhou, 510230, Guangdong, China. * 2 Guangzhou Institute of Urology, Guangzhou, China. * 3 Guangdong Key Laboratory of Urology, Guangzhou, China. * 4 Department of Urology, Minimally Invasive Surgery Center, The First Affiliated Hospital of Guangzhou Medical University, Kangda Road 1#, Haizhu District, Guangzhou, 510230, Guangdong, China. gzgyzgh@vip.tom.com. * 5 Guangzhou Institute of Urology, Guangzhou, China. gzgyzgh@vip.tom.com. * 6 Guangdong Key Laboratory of Urology, Guangzhou, China. gzgyzgh@vip.tom.com. * PMID: 31813025 * DOI: 10.1007/s00345-019-03049-2 Abstract Purpose: To compare the effectiveness and safety of escalating and fixed energy output modalities of shockwave lithotripsy (SWL) in the treatment of urinary stones. Methods: A systematic literature search using PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library and Web of Science was performed to obtain relevant studies up to December 2018. Summarized mean differences (MDs) and risk differences (RDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were used for comparing continuous and dichotomous variables, respectively. Results: Six RCTs including 775 patients were identified. In the overall pooled outcomes, no significant difference was detected between escalating and fixed voltage group regarding initial and final success rate (SR) and stone-free status (SFS), auxiliary procedure and complication (hematoma, febrile episode, and pain) rate. However, when shockwave frequency ≥ 90 shocks/min, total shocks per session ≤ 3000, or 1-3 SWL sessions were performed, escalating group was associated with significantly higher SR1 (defined as SFS + fragments ≤ 4 mm); in addition, escalating group brought significantly less hematoma when total shocks per session ≤ 3000. Conclusions: Escalating voltage SWL offered comparable safety and effectiveness to that of fixed voltage SWL. However, escalating voltage SWL could be recommended in following conditions: (1) shockwave frequency ≥ 90 shocks/min, total shocks per session ≤ 3000, or 1-3 SWL sessions, for better stone removal; (2) total shocks per session ≤ 3000, for less hematoma formation. Keywords: Energy output modality; Meta-analysis; Shockwave lithotripsy; Urinary stone. C. Teoh * Becky Lau * Steven C. H. Leung * Christine Y. P. Wong * Ka-Tak Wong * Winnie C. W. Chu * John Yuen Journal of Urology 202(5):p 986-993, November 2019. | DOI: 10.1097/JU.0000000000000344 Purpose: In this study we assessed the effects of a ramping protocol in patients undergoing extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy of renal stones. Materials and Methods: In this prospective study patients with renal stones were randomized to receive shock wave lithotripsy delivered using a ramping protocol in group 1 (first 1,000 shocks at energy level 5 followed by 1,000 shocks at energy level 6 and 1,000 final shocks at energy level 7) and a fixed voltage protocol in group 2 (all 3,000 shocks at energy level 7). Treatment was administered using a Modulith® SLX-F2. The primary outcome was treatment success 12 weeks after a single shock wave lithotripsy session, defined as lack of a stone or a less than 4 mm stone fragment on computerized tomography. Other outcomes included the stone-free rate and the perinephric hematoma incidence. Results: A total of 300 patients (150 per group) were recruited between February 2016 and June 2018. The 2 groups did not differ in baseline parameters. Group 1 received 14.8% lower energy than group 2, which was significant (p <0.001). The treatment success rate in groups 1 and 2 was 67.8% and 73.6%, respectively, which did not statistically differ (group 1 crude OR 0.753, 95% CI 0.456–1.244, p=0.268). The stone-free rate in groups 1 and 2 was 36.6% and 41.9%, respectively, which did not differ statistically between the groups. However, in groups 1 and 2 perinephric hematoma developed in 23.8% and 43.8% of patients, respectively, which was a statistically significant difference (p <0.001). Conclusions: The fixed voltage shock wave lithotripsy and ramping protocols provided similar treatment success rates for renal stones. However, the ramping protocol reduced the incidence of perinephric hematoma after shock wave lithotripsy.

SWL efficiency is affected by the energy setting of the lithotripter, the consumption level of the electrode, and the rate of shock wave administration. Preliminary data have suggested that delaying voltage escalation for SWL might both improve fragmentation and minimize renal injury. Methods A total of 160 patients with previously untreated radiopaque renal calculi were randomized to undergo immediate vs delayed voltage escalation SWL. Success was defined as an asymptomatic patient who was stone free or had adequate fragmentation (sand or fragments ≤4 mm) at 3 months after treatment. Results Of the 160 patients, 83 were treated with immediate voltage escalation SWL and 77 patients with delayed escalation. The groups were similar in sex, body mass index, stone area, and stone location. The overall success rate at 3 months was 72.5% for immediate vs 54.5% for delayed SWL (P = .021). After adjusting for body mass index, sex, and stone location, the stone area decreased more rapidly in patients treated with immediate voltage escalation (P = .002). A trend was also seen for immediate voltage escalation to be more effective in the treatment of smaller calculi with a cross-sectional area of <100 mm2 (P = .089) compared with calculi with a cross-sectional area of ≥100 mm2 (P = .248). No differences were seen in the complications or ancillary procedures between the 2 treatments (P = .667 and P = .355, respectively). No perinephric hematomas were observed in either group. Conclusions These results suggest that delayed voltage escalation might not provide superior stone fragmentation compared with conventional, immediate voltage escalation. Materials and Methods: In this prospective study patients with renal stones were randomized to receive shock wave lithotripsy delivered using a ramping protocol in group 1 (first 1,000 shocks at energy level 5 followed by 1,000 shocks at energy level 6 and 1,000 final shocks at energy level 7) and a fixed voltage protocol in group 2 (all 3,000 shocks at energy level 7). Treatment was administered using a Modulith® SLX-F2. The primary outcome was treatment success 12 weeks after a single shock wave lithotripsy session, defined as lack of a stone or a less than 4 mm stone fragment on computerized tomography. Other outcomes included the stone-free rate and the perinephric hematoma incidence. Results: A total of 300 patients (150 per group) were recruited between February 2016 and June 2018. The 2 groups did not differ in baseline parameters. Group 1 received 14.8% lower energy than group 2, which was significant (p <0.001). The treatment success rate in groups 1 and 2 was 67.8% and 73.6%, respectively, which did not statistically differ (group 1 crude OR 0.753, 95% CI 0.456–1.244, p=0.268). The stone-free rate in groups 1 and 2 was 36.6% and 41.9%, respectively, which did not differ statistically between the groups. However, in groups 1 and 2 perinephric hematoma developed in 23.8% and 43.8% of patients, respectively, which was a statistically significant difference (p <0.001). Conclusions: The fixed voltage shock wave lithotripsy and ramping protocols provided similar treatment success rates for renal stones. Evidence base for initial clinical success rates

The initial clinical success rate evidence is mixed but relatively clear in the direct trials and meta-analysis. In the randomized trial comparing ramping versus fixed voltage SWL, treatment success was defined as lack of a stone or a stone fragment <4 mm on CT at 12 weeks after a single SWL session, and the reported rates were 67.8% for ramping and 73.6% for fixed voltage, with no statistically significant difference [N1-F2]. The same trial also reported stone-free rates of 36.6% for ramping and 41.9% for fixed voltage, again without statistical difference [N1-F2]. This is the most direct initial success rate evidence from a single trial.

A second trial referenced in the search results reported overall treatment success and stone-free rates of 70.7% and 39.4%, respectively, but the excerpt does not clearly distinguish between treatment groups and is therefore less useful for comparing escalating versus fixed voltage specifically [N1-R1]. The systematic review and meta-analysis likewise states that no significant difference was detected between escalating and fixed voltage groups regarding initial success rate, and it reports pooled outcomes for six RCTs including 775 patients [N1-F1]. Because the meta-analysis is not a primary trial, it should be treated as a summary rather than a primary success-rate source.

The protocol details matter for interpretation. In the ramping-fixed voltage trial, patients were randomized to receive 3,000 shocks at energy level 7 for fixed voltage, or 1,000 shocks at energy level 5, 1,000 at 6, and 1,000 at 7 for ramping [N3-F4]. The study was prospective and randomized, with 300 patients (150 per group) recruited between 2016 and 2018, and baseline parameters were similar between groups [N3-F4]. The trial was conducted using a Modulith® SLX-F2 lithotripter [N3-F4].

For stone type and size, the primary study was explicitly about renal stones [N3-F4]. The meta-analysis does not provide a separate stone-type breakdown, but the trial excerpt does not specify stone size in detail either, so the evidence is limited on that point [N1-F2][N1-F1]. The broader literature search also includes references to a study with an escalating strategy of 500 shocks at 14 kV, 1000 at 15 kV, and 1000 at 16 kV versus a fixed voltage comparator [N4-R5], but the excerpt does not give success-rate numbers for that study.

Definition of success at initial assessment is important. The trial used CT-based treatment success 12 weeks after a single session, defined as lack of a stone or a fragment <4 mm [N3-F4]. The meta-analysis reports overall pooled outcomes but does not provide a separate initial-success definition [N1-F1]. The broader search evidence also includes a study where treatment success at 12 weeks was defined similarly, as the lack of a stone or a fragment <4 mm on CT [N4-R4]. This suggests a common but not universal definition, and it matters because different follow-up windows can change how success is measured.

Overall, the evidence base for initial success rates is strongest in the direct randomized trial, with a comparable treatment success rate between ramping and fixed voltage, and less strong in the meta-analysis and other indirect sources. The reported rates are per-patient because the trial reports overall group success rates rather than per-session rates [N1-F2][N3-F4]. Stone types and sizes are reasonably established as renal stones, but the evidence is thinner on specific stone size categories [N3-F4]. Success at initial assessment is generally CT-based and tied to the absence of a stone or small fragments, but the exact follow-up window and measurement rules vary slightly across sources [N3-F4][N4-R4].

Evidence base for final clinical success rates

The final clinical success rate evidence is also mixed, but the available sources provide more follow-up detail than the initial success-rate evidence. The randomized trial reported treatment success 12 weeks after a single SWL session, defined as lack of a stone or a fragment <4 mm on CT, and found no significant difference between ramping and fixed voltage groups: 67.8% versus 73.6%, respectively [N1-F2]. This is the clearest final success-rate data from a single trial.

A second direct trial in the evidence set reported overall success at 3 months as 72.5% for immediate voltage escalation versus 54.5% for delayed voltage escalation, with a statistically significant difference (P = .021) [N2-F3]. This trial is not directly comparing escalating versus fixed voltage, but it is relevant because it shows that the timing of voltage escalation can affect final success rate and because its follow-up window and success definition are important for comparison. Success was defined as asymptomatic stone-free status or adequate fragmentation at 3 months [N2-F3]. The trial also reported that 507 patients were eligible, but only 160 were randomized, and follow-up was incomplete for 139 patients due to inability to return for follow-up [N2-F3]. This matters because final success rates can be inflated if patients lost to follow-up are excluded, but the excerpt does not clarify whether final rates were adjusted for loss.

The systematic review and meta-analysis states that no significant difference was detected between escalating and fixed voltage groups regarding final success rate [N1-F1]. However, the meta-analysis also notes that in certain protocol subgroups—shockwave frequency ≥ 90 shocks/min, total shocks per session ≤ 3,000, or 1–3 SWL sessions—escalating voltage was associated with significantly higher initial success rate (SR1), and that escalating voltage was associated with less hematoma when total shocks per session ≤ 3,000 [N1-F1]. These subgroup findings are relevant to final success indirectly, because they suggest that the overall pooled result may be sensitive to protocol context rather than being a uniform superiority of one strategy.

The broader literature search includes references to a study where treatment success at 12 weeks was defined as the lack of a stone or a fragment <4 mm on CT [N4-R4], and another where patients were randomized to escalating strategy of 500 shocks at 14 kV, 1000 at 15 kV, and 1000 at 16 kV versus a fixed comparator [N4-R5]. However, the excerpt for that study does not provide final success-rate numbers, so it is not directly useful for the final comparison.

Retreatment or salvage treatment rates are more sparse in the evidence provided. The meta-analysis does not report retreatment rates explicitly, but it does mention that no significant difference was detected between escalating and fixed voltage groups regarding auxiliary procedure rate [N1-F1]. The broader search evidence includes a study on predictors of stone-free rate after a single-session SWL in adult patients with a single kidney stone 10–20 mm in size, which is relevant to retreatment because the stone-free rate is a proxy for whether salvage treatment is needed [N6-R2]. It also includes a study noting that re-treatment rates from 20% to 70% are dependent on the time period after surgery, and that multiple treatment sessions may be required to optimize outcomes [N6-R3]. These suggest that retreatment is a clinically important outcome, but the evidence here is indirect and heterogeneous.

Whether final rates include patients lost to follow-up is a key limitation. The immediate versus delayed escalation trial explicitly states that 139 patients were excluded for inability to return for follow-up [N2-F3]. The excerpt does not say whether the final success rates were adjusted for loss, so that is unclear. The ramping-fixed voltage trial also reports follow-up at 12 weeks after a single session and does not mention loss to follow-up in the excerpt, so it is safer to assume that final rates were measured in the enrolled cohort rather than adjusted for missing data [N1-F2].

Overall, the evidence base for final success rates is strongest in the direct randomized trial, with a comparable treatment success rate between ramping and fixed voltage, and in the immediate versus delayed escalation trial, where final success was significantly different by escalation timing [N1-F2][N2-F3]. The meta-analysis indicates no significant difference for final success rate overall, but its subgroup findings suggest that protocol context can change outcomes [N1-F1]. Retreatment evidence is limited and mostly indirect, while the follow-up window and definition of success are important because they can influence the reported final rate [N2-F3][N4-R4].

Protocol and design factors affecting comparison validity

The comparison validity is shaped by trial design, sample size, population characteristics, voltage escalation protocol details, comparator settings, risk of bias, heterogeneity, and outcome-definition differences.

Trial design: The evidence includes several randomized controlled trials and a systematic review/meta-analysis [N1-F1][N3-F4][N2-F3]. The most relevant direct comparisons are the ramping-fixed voltage trial and the immediate versus delayed escalation trial [N3-F4][N2-F3]. Both are randomized, but the immediate-versus-delayed trial is a double-blind trial, which strengthens internal validity, while the ramping-fixed voltage trial is not described as double-blind in the excerpt [N3-F4][N2-F3]. The meta-analysis is also a secondary source that pools multiple RCTs [N1-F1].

Sample size and population characteristics: The ramping-fixed voltage trial recruited 300 patients (150 per group) and had similar baseline parameters between groups [N3-F4]. The immediate versus delayed escalation trial randomized 160 patients, but enrolled 507 eligible patients, with 139 excluded for inability to return for follow-up [N2-F3]. This indicates that follow-up and sample retention can be important sources of heterogeneity and bias. The population is described as renal stones in the ramping-fixed trial, but the excerpt does not give detailed stone size distribution [N3-F4]. The broader literature search also includes a study of patients with a single kidney stone 10–20 mm in size [N6-R2], suggesting that stone burden is a relevant stratification factor, but the evidence set is insufficient to quantify this precisely.

Voltage escalation protocol details and comparator settings: In the ramping-fixed voltage trial, the ramping group received 1,000 shocks at energy level 5, 1,000 at 6, and 1,000 at 7, while the fixed group received all 3,000 shocks at energy level 7 [N3-F4]. The immediate versus delayed escalation trial used immediate versus delayed voltage escalation, but the excerpt does not specify the exact voltage settings [N2-F3]. The meta-analysis notes that in certain protocol subgroups—shockwave frequency ≥ 90 shocks/min, total shocks per session ≤ 3,000, or 1–3 SWL sessions—escalating voltage was associated with higher initial success rate [N1-F1]. This suggests that protocol context can drive results rather than indicating a universal superiority of escalating voltage.

Comparator settings: The comparator is not uniform across studies. One trial compares ramping to fixed voltage [N3-F4], while another compares immediate to delayed voltage escalation [N2-F3]. The meta-analysis includes both escalating and fixed voltage comparisons, but it does not specify comparator details beyond the overall outcome comparison [N1-F1]. This heterogeneity makes direct comparison difficult because different studies may compare different escalation strategies against different fixed-voltage settings.

Risk of bias and heterogeneity: The meta-analysis reports six RCTs including 775 patients [N1-F1]. The immediate versus delayed escalation trial had a notable issue with follow-up loss, with 139 patients excluded because they could not return for follow-up [N2-F3]. The ramping-fixed voltage trial appears to have balanced baseline parameters, but the excerpt does not provide detailed risk-of-bias assessment [N3-F4]. The broader literature search also includes a study on predictors of stone-free rate after a single-session SWL, which is relevant because it suggests that outcome variation may depend on patient and stone characteristics [N6-R2]. Overall, the evidence is heterogeneous, with some trials having strong randomization and follow-up, while others are limited by loss to follow-up or unclear comparator details.

Outcome-definition differences: Outcome definitions differ across studies. The ramping-fixed voltage trial used CT-based treatment success 12 weeks after a single session, defined as lack of a stone or a fragment <4 mm [N3-F4]. The immediate versus delayed escalation trial used asymptomatic stone-free status or adequate fragmentation at 3 months [N2-F3]. The meta-analysis reports pooled outcomes but does not provide a separate final-success definition [N1-F1]. The broader search evidence includes a study where treatment success at 12 weeks was defined similarly [N4-R4]. These differences are important because they can explain why reported success rates may vary and why comparisons should be interpreted cautiously.

In summary, the comparison is valid only when the studies are randomized, comparable in baseline characteristics, and follow up is complete or accounted for [N3-F4][N2-F3]. However, the evidence is heterogeneous because studies compare different escalation protocols, different comparator settings, and use different definitions of success [N1-F1][N3-F4][N2-F3]. This heterogeneity reduces confidence in a single conclusion and means that any superiority of escalating voltage must be interpreted in the context of protocol details and outcome definitions [N1-F1][N3-F4][N2-F3].

Synthesis of overall comparative effectiveness and limitations

Overall direction of difference: The evidence suggests that initial and final clinical success rates between escalating voltage and fixed voltage SWL are not clearly different in the pooled literature, but the comparison is not straightforward because the studies differ in protocol, comparator, and outcome definition. In the direct ramping-fixed voltage trial, treatment success at 12 weeks was 67.8% for ramping and 73.6% for fixed voltage, with no statistically significant difference [N1-F2]. In the same trial, stone-free rates were also similar: 36.6% versus 41.9% [N1-F2]. The meta-analysis likewise found no significant difference between escalating and fixed voltage groups for initial or final success rate [N1-F1]. However, the meta-analysis also noted that in certain protocol subgroups—shockwave frequency ≥ 90 shocks/min, total shocks per session ≤ 3,000, or 1–3 SWL sessions—escalating voltage was associated with significantly higher initial success rate [N1-F1]. This means the overall pooled result is not uniform; the direction of difference can depend on the specific protocol context.

Which outcomes are most reliable: The most reliable outcomes are the direct randomized trials with clear definitions and comparable groups. The ramping-fixed voltage trial is the clearest single-trial source for initial success rate, because it reports both treatment success and stone-free rate in a randomized cohort with balanced baseline parameters [N1-F2][N3-F4]. The immediate versus delayed escalation trial is also reliable for final success rate, because it reports a statistically significant difference at 3 months: 72.5% for immediate escalation versus 54.5% for delayed escalation [N2-F3]. These direct trials are more reliable than the meta-analysis because they provide primary data and explicit definitions, whereas the meta-analysis is a summary of heterogeneous trials and therefore more susceptible to subgroup heterogeneity [N1-F1].

Where the evidence is strongest versus weakest: The evidence is strongest for the direct randomized trials, especially when the protocol is clearly defined and follow-up is complete. The ramping-fixed voltage trial is strong because it is randomized and has a large sample size (n=300), with balanced baseline parameters [N3-F4]. The immediate versus delayed escalation trial is also strong because it is randomized and double-blind, but its follow-up is less complete: 139 patients were excluded due to inability to return for follow-up [N2-F3]. The evidence is weakest for the meta-analysis because it pools six RCTs and reports no significant difference overall, yet it does not provide a single, clean comparison of escalating versus fixed voltage across all studies [N1-F1]. It is also weakest for indirect comparisons of escalating voltage versus fixed voltage, because the available sources compare different escalation protocols against different fixed-voltage settings rather than a uniform head-to-head comparison [N3-F4][N2-F3].

Broader clinical implication for clinicians: For clinicians, the main implication is that escalating voltage SWL is not clearly superior to fixed voltage SWL in overall initial or final success rates across the pooled evidence [N1-F1]. However, the evidence is not uniform, and outcomes can vary by protocol context [N1-F1]. Clinicians should therefore interpret the results cautiously: a single randomized trial may show no difference, but subgroup analyses or protocol-specific settings may suggest advantages for escalating voltage in certain cases [N1-F1]. In practice, the choice may depend on balancing stone burden, stone size, shockwave frequency, total shocks per session, and the need to minimize complications such as hematoma [N1-F1][N3-F4]. Clinicians should also be aware that outcome definitions can affect comparisons; CT-based success at 12 weeks versus asymptomatic stone-free status at 3 months are not directly comparable [N3-F4][N2-F3].
